known: The status API calls GetAllEndpointStatuses on a miss of a 10s-TTL cache
Postgres schema lacks indexes on endpoint_results(endpoint_id), endpoint_result_conditions(endpoint_result_id) and endpoint_events(endpoint_id)
unknown: Deployed storage type and caching setting
assumed: The reported DB-server CPU implies Postgres
derived: Up to 4 queries per endpoint plus 1 per cache miss, from the loop in getEndpointStatusByKey

root_causes.description: Key listing scans the full results table on every uncached load
Postgres schema omits indexes on foreign-key lookup columns
Status assembly issues per-endpoint queries in a loop

findings.problem: The key-listing query that starts every uncached dashboard load joins endpoints to endpoint_results and applies DISTINCT. It has to read every non-suite result row of every endpoint, so its cost follows total stored results, not the page size or endpoint count.
findings.performance_principle: Work done per request should be proportional to what is returned, not to the volume of retained history.

evidence.statement: SELECT DISTINCT e.endpoint_key FROM endpoints e INNER JOIN endpoint_results er ON ... WHERE er.suite_result_id IS NULL ORDER BY e.endpoint_key, run inside GetAllEndpointStatuses on each cache miss.
GetAllEndpointStatuses calls getAllEndpointKeys first, then loops over the keys.
The API handler calls store.Get().GetAllEndpointStatuses on a miss of a 10s-TTL cache. No runtime evidence was supplied.

findings.conditions: Many past results retained per endpoint (the reported condition) and cache misses on the 10s API cache. Rows examined is roughly endpoints x results retained per endpoint; the retention limit is storage maximum-number-of-results, whose default is 100 (storage/config.go:8).

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for an existence check, a LIMIT, or a pre-aggregated endpoint list; none exists. The only filter is IS NULL on suite_result_id, which the indexes cannot make selective.
Retention is capped per endpoint by deleteOldEndpointResults, so growth is bounded by the configured maximum, but that maximum is the variable the operators report as large.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: With the default of 100 results and few endpoints the scan is cheap. The 10s API cache and the write-through cache absorb repeat requests. Nothing here proves it dominates DB CPU; no plan was supplied.
findings.recommendation: Derive the key list without scanning the results table, for example from endpoints alone with an EXISTS check that stops at the first match per endpoint, or keep a flag on endpoints. Either makes cost follow endpoints, not retained results.

alternatives.option: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM endpoint_results WHERE endpoint_id = e.endpoint_id AND suite_result_id IS NULL) over endpoints
alternatives.why: Stops at the first match per endpoint and needs only an index on endpoint_id (see PERF-002).
Masks the work and adds staleness to the status page without removing it.

findings.trade_offs: The EXISTS form must keep the exclusion of suite-only endpoints. A flag column adds a write-path update and a migration.

validation.metric: Rows read and execution time of the key-listing query on a copy of production data with many results per endpoint
validation.expectation: Rows examined should fall from the order of the results table to the order of the endpoints table.
validation.falsifier: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) already shows an index-only or semi-join plan that touches roughly one row per endpoint.
validation.guard: A benchmark in storage/store/store_bench_test.go with many results per endpoint, asserting cost stays flat as results grow.

commands.command: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT DISTINCT e.endpoint_key FROM endpoints e INNER JOIN endpoint_results er ON e.endpoint_id = er.endpoint_id WHERE er.suite_result_id IS NULL ORDER BY e.endpoint_key;
commands.purpose: Show the plan and rows read; run on a restored copy.

findings.problem: The Postgres schema creates no index on endpoint_results(endpoint_id), endpoint_result_conditions(endpoint_result_id) or endpoint_events(endpoint_id). Postgres does not index foreign-key columns automatically, and the dashboard path filters on all three. The SQLite schema does index the first two (specific_sqlite.go:115 and :127).
findings.performance_principle: A selective lookup should be answered by an access path proportional to the matching rows, not by scanning the table.

evidence.statement: Postgres index statements: only suite_results_suite_id_idx and endpoint_results_suite_result_id_idx are created; endpoint_uptimes has an implicit UNIQUE(endpoint_id, hour_unix_timestamp) index.
Results query: WHERE endpoint_id = $1 ORDER BY endpoint_result_id DESC LIMIT/OFFSET, run once per endpoint.
Condition lookup: WHERE endpoint_result_id IN (...) over endpoint_result_conditions, run once per endpoint; it is the largest table (one or more rows per result).
deleteOldEndpointResults repeats an endpoint_id filter with a NOT IN subquery on each insert.

findings.conditions: Postgres storage (a separate DB server is implied by the report; SQLite is in-process) with many retained results per endpoint. The planner's real choice is unknown: for the results query it may walk the primary key backwards filtering on endpoint_id, cheap for recently active endpoints and costly for sparse ones. The condition lookup has no such shortcut.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched storage/store/sql for CREATE INDEX statements and migrations on these columns; none exist for Postgres.
The planner might pick a backward primary-key scan for the results query. That lowers certainty on that query only, so confidence is capped at Medium.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If an index was added out of band, or the primary-key scan terminates early, the effect is smaller. Small tables make a sequential scan cheap, and the write-through cache hides repeated reads.
findings.recommendation: Add indexes on endpoint_results(endpoint_id), endpoint_result_conditions(endpoint_result_id) and endpoint_events(endpoint_id) for Postgres, mirroring SQLite, via CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS in createPostgresSchema.

alternatives.why: Matches the access patterns in the code and already exists in the SQLite schema.
Could serve the ordered LIMIT directly but costs more write space; choose only if a plan shows the simple index is not enough.

findings.trade_offs: Each index adds write cost and storage on insert-heavy tables. Building indexes on large existing tables locks writes unless built concurrently.

validation.metric: Plan node type and buffers read for the results and condition queries per endpoint, before and after
validation.expectation: Sequential scans on endpoint_results and endpoint_result_conditions are replaced by index scans.
validation.falsifier: EXPLAIN already shows index scans on these columns, or an out-of-band index exists in pg_indexes.
validation.guard: A schema test asserting the index set for the Postgres driver.

commands.command: SELECT tablename, indexname, indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename IN ('endpoint_results','endpoint_result_conditions','endpoint_events');
commands.purpose: Confirm which indexes exist on the live database before changing anything.

commands.command: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT endpoint_result_id, condition, success FROM endpoint_result_conditions WHERE endpoint_result_id IN (1,2,3);
commands.purpose: Check the scan type for the condition lookup; substitute real ids on a restored copy.

findings.problem: GetAllEndpointStatuses runs several queries per endpoint serially in one transaction (id lookup, events, results, plus a conditions lookup), so round trips grow linearly with the endpoint count.
findings.performance_principle: Round trips per request should not scale with the number of returned entities.

evidence.statement: Loop over keys calling getEndpointStatusByKey, which issues getEndpointIDGroupAndNameByKey, getEndpointEventsByEndpointID and getEndpointResultsByEndpointID (the last with a follow-up conditions query).
Per-key errors are swallowed by continue, so a failing query is silent.

findings.conditions: Many endpoints and a miss on the 10s API cache. Derived: up to 4 queries per endpoint plus 1 for the key list; latency impact depends on network distance to the DB, which is unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: The write-through cache (up to 10000 entries) can serve getEndpointStatusByKey without queries when enabled; whether it is enabled depends on config not examined.
Single transaction on one connection, so no pool exhaustion from the loop itself.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: A local or low-latency DB with few endpoints makes the loop cheap, and caches sit on the path. It matters most together with PERF-002, where each per-endpoint query is also slow.
findings.recommendation: Batch by fetching events and results for all keys in a few set-based queries (window function over endpoint_id, one IN list), or pre-warm the write-through cache.

alternatives.option: Set-based queries using ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY endpoint_id)
alternatives.why: Removes per-endpoint round trips without adding state.
Only helps when enabled and warm; cold start and 10s API cache expiry still pay the full cost.

findings.trade_offs: More complex SQL and a different pagination implementation; larger result sets per query.

validation.metric: Number of queries issued per GET of the endpoint statuses API on a cache miss
validation.expectation: Query count should stop growing with endpoint count.
validation.falsifier: Query logging shows the write-through cache serves nearly all lookups on an API cache miss.
validation.guard: A test counting queries against a store seeded with N endpoints.

considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Quadratic copy, but bounded by the page size, which is clamped to the configured maximum; negligible next to query cost.
